To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the Cincinnati Arch is a single basin with a single depositional system; (ii) meter-scale shelly-mud cycles are basin-wide; (iii) the Cincinnati Arch was a shallow, stormy, carbonate-dominated system with abundant mud supply; (iv) the Cincinnati Arch did not have a “tempestite belt” that tracked storm intensity and/or sea level; (v) the Cincinnati Arch had a “mud belt” that tracked the amount of sediment supply; and
meter-scale cycles in the Upper Ordvovician of the Cincinnati Arch are the product of episodic sedimentary starvation rather than winnowing of fair-weather sediments by storms or other events.
(i) meter-scale shelly-mud alternations in the Cincinnati Arch are non-Waltherian facies; and (ii) they represent episodes of siliciclastics starvation rather than winnowing by turbulence events
In summary, our research is concerned with
the origin of shell-rich deposits in mudstones.
the origin and stratigraphic significance of shell beds and cycles.
the origin of meter-scale cycles in the Cincinnati Arch and the broader Upper Ordovician Cincinnati Series.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Cincinnati succession represents a series of shallow marine shelf deposits, with a variety of sedimentological and biotic responses to episodic fluctuations in sediment supply, rather than a series of storm deposits.
the “episodical starvation model” is supported by all of the available evidence, and that the “storm winnowing model” is not supported by any of the available evidence.
, in the absence of other evidence, shell beds are not necessarily tempestites.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in the Cincinnati region, the episodic starvation model is supported by the following: (1) shell beds are not tempestites; (2) meter-scale cycles are not produced by varying storm intensity; (3) meter-scale cycles represent basin-wide, not lateral, changes in sedimentary processes; (4) meter-scale cycles reflect basin-wide changes in siliciclastic supply, not sea-level change; and (5) shell-rich intervals are not produced by winnowing, but instead
the Cincinnati Arch is characterized by a “tempestite paradox,” i.e. a lack of evidence for tempestites in the form of winnowed shell beds.
, in the Cincinnati Arch area, the episodic starvation model provides a more parsimonious and realistic explanation for the origin of shelly-muddy cycles than the tempestite proximally model.
The main takeaway from our work is that
shell beds and shell-rich cycles in mudstones are time-specific, rather than local, facies.
the episodic starvation model is more consistent than the tempestite proximally model with the observed patterns of facies distribution, amalgamation, and condensation.
shell-rich beds and mud-dominated beds are not mutually exclusive.
